questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Centre and radius of a circle
questions.learningObjective: name the two facts that determine a circle
questions.stem: A gardener marks out a lawn circle by driving one stake into the ground and looping a rope of length 6 meters around it before driving a second stake. Which two facts together determine the circle that method draws?

options.text: The centre at the first stake, and the radius fixed at 6 meters
The centre at the first stake, and the diameter fixed at 6 meters
options.misconception: reads the rope length as the diameter, so the drawn circle has half the intended radius

options.text: A point on the rim at the first stake, and the radius fixed at 6 meters
options.misconception: puts the centre of the circle on the rim instead of at the stake

options.text: The centre 6 meters from the first stake, and a radius of unknown length
options.misconception: assumes the radius is missing when only the centre still needs naming

questions.explanation: A circle is fully located by its centre and its radius: the centre says where the middle of the circle sits, and the radius says how far the boundary is from that middle. The first stake supplies the centre and the rope length supplies the radius, so those two facts fix every point of the circle. Reading the rope as a diameter would draw a circle with half the intended radius, and leaving the radius unspecified would leave an endless family of circles around the same stake.
questions.hint: Ask what a pair of compasses needs to be told before it can draw anything.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Centre-radius equation of a circle
questions.learningObjective: read the centre and radius out of a centre-radius equation
questions.stem: A circular arena is modelled by the equation (x - 2)^2 + (y + 5)^2 = 64, where both coordinates are measured in meters. What do the three parts of this equation stand for?

options.text: The centre sits at (2, -5) and the radius is 8 meters
The centre sits at (-2, 5) and the radius is 8 meters
options.misconception: reads the sign inside a bracket as the coordinate itself rather than as a subtraction

options.text: The centre sits at (2, -5) and the radius is 64 meters
options.misconception: takes the number on the right of the equation as the radius instead of its square root

options.text: The centre sits at (0, 0) and the radius is 8 meters
options.misconception: assumes a shifted equation still describes a circle centred on the origin

questions.explanation: In centre-radius form each bracket measures how far a point lies from the centre along that axis, so (x - 2) is the horizontal offset from 2 and (y + 5) is the vertical offset from -5. Squaring the two offsets and adding them produces the square of the straight-line distance from the centre, and the right-hand side is that square, so the radius is the square root of 64, which is 8. Whatever sign appears inside a bracket is subtracted, which is why the vertical centre coordinate is -5 rather than 5.
questions.hint: The right-hand side is the square of the radius, not the radius itself.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Distance from a centre to a point
questions.learningObjective: measure how far a point lies from the centre of a circle
questions.stem: A circular pond has its centre at the origin of a survey grid, with every distance on the grid measured in meters. A marker buoy floats at the point (15, 20). How many meters is that buoy from the centre of the pond? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The distance from the origin to (15, 20) is the square root of 15 squared plus 20 squared, and 15 squared is 225 while 20 squared is 400, so the sum is 625 and its square root is 25 meters. The legs 15 and 20 form the 3-4-5 pattern scaled by 5, which confirms the answer is 5 times 5, that is 25. The pond's radius is 25 meters, so the buoy sits exactly on the shore rather than inside or beyond it.
questions.hint: Square each coordinate, add the two squares, then take the square root of the total.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Perpendicular from the centre to a chord
questions.learningObjective: use the perpendicular from a centre to show that a chord is bisected
questions.stem: A straight line cuts a chord across a circular pond, and a segment drawn from the centre of the pond down to that chord meets it at a right angle. What does the right angle guarantee about the two pieces of the chord?

options.text: The two pieces are equal, because a perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord
The two pieces are equal, because any segment from the centre bisects a chord
options.misconception: believes every radius that meets a chord bisects it, even a slanted one

options.text: The two pieces are equal, because the chord measures twice the centre-to-chord distance
options.misconception: confuses the length of the chord with twice the perpendicular distance to it

options.text: The two pieces are unequal, because the perpendicular only finds the nearest point
options.misconception: denies the bisecting property of a perpendicular dropped from the centre

questions.explanation: The two ends of a chord are the same distance from the centre, and the set of points equidistant from two fixed endpoints is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them, so the centre already lies on the perpendicular bisector of every chord. The right angle is the extra condition that matters: a slanted radius meeting the chord generally lands off the midpoint, while a perpendicular from the centre lands on it and splits the chord into equal halves. The perpendicular distance from the centre is a separate quantity, found with the Pythagorean theorem.
questions.hint: The centre is equidistant from the two ends of any chord. Which line collects such points?

questions.topic: Centre-to-chord distance
questions.learningObjective: find the distance from a centre to a chord from the radius and chord length
questions.stem: A circular sign has a radius of 13 inches, and a straight metal bar laid across the sign forms a chord 24 inches long. How many inches is the perpendicular distance from the centre of the sign down to that bar? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The perpendicular from the centre lands on the midpoint of the chord, so the 24 inch chord becomes two 12 inch halves and the centre, the midpoint, and one chord end form a right triangle with the 13 inch radius as its hypotenuse. The distance is the square root of 13 squared minus 12 squared, that is the square root of 169 minus 144, which is the square root of 25, so 5 inches. The triple 5, 12, 13 confirms it because 25 plus 144 equals 169.
questions.hint: Halve the chord, then use the radius as the hypotenuse of a right triangle.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Diameter perpendicular to a chord
questions.learningObjective: state why a diameter meeting a chord at a right angle bisects it
questions.stem: A steel wheel rests on a rail, and a straight rod held across the wheel touches the rim at two points 20 centimeters apart. A line through the centre, drawn at a right angle to the rod, cuts that rod in half. Which statement accounts for the cut?

options.text: Any diameter drawn at a right angle to a chord passes through that chord's midpoint
Any diameter drawn at all will pass through the midpoint of the chord it meets
options.misconception: believes every diameter, at any angle, bisects a chord it happens to cross

options.text: A chord's midpoint is always half a diameter's length out from the rim
options.misconception: confuses a midpoint position with a distance to be counted in half units

options.text: A diameter can only cut a chord in half when the two lengths are equal
options.misconception: thinks a diameter must match the chord in length to bisect it

questions.explanation: The centre of a circle is the same distance from the two ends of every chord, so it lies on the perpendicular bisector of each chord. The diameter running at a right angle to a chord is exactly that perpendicular bisector, and it therefore meets the chord at the midpoint. The angle of crossing decides the outcome: a diameter at a slant cuts the chord away from its centre. No equality of lengths between diameter and chord is required for the bisecting to happen.
questions.hint: Start from the fact that the centre is equidistant from both chord ends.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Tangent and radius at contact
questions.learningObjective: state the angle a tangent makes with the radius to its point of contact
questions.stem: A round coin lies flat on a table and a straight ruler is laid against its edge so that it touches the coin at one point and lifts clear everywhere else. How does the ruler meet the radius drawn to that contact point?

options.text: They meet at a right angle, which is what makes the ruler a tangent line
They meet at an angle below a right angle, since the ruler leans away
options.misconception: believes the lean of the ruler forces the meeting angle to be acute

options.text: They are the same segment, since the ruler starts where the radius starts
options.misconception: confuses a tangent line with the radius it touches at a single point

options.text: They never meet at all, since a tangent holds a fixed gap from the circle
options.misconception: thinks a tangent keeps a constant distance from the circle instead of touching it

questions.explanation: A tangent meets a circle at exactly one point, and at that point it is perpendicular to the radius drawn to it. The reason is that any line through a point of the circle that is not perpendicular to the radius cuts the circle a second time, while the perpendicular direction stays outside the disk for every step away from the contact point. The ruler therefore makes a 90 degree angle with the radius there. A tangent does touch the circle, so there is no gap for it to hold open.
questions.hint: Ask which single direction from a point on a circle never re-enters the circle.

questions.topic: Length of a tangent segment
questions.learningObjective: find the length of a tangent drawn from an external point
questions.stem: A circular fountain has a radius of 15 meters. A maintenance post stands 25 meters away from the fountain's centre, and a straight taut cable runs from the post to the fountain's rim, just touching it. How many meters long is that cable? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The cable is a tangent segment, so the radius drawn to the point of contact is perpendicular to the cable. That makes a right triangle whose hypotenuse is the 25 meter centre-to-post distance and whose one leg is the 15 meter radius, with the cable as the remaining leg. The cable is the square root of 25 squared minus 15 squared, that is the square root of 625 minus 225, which is the square root of 400, giving 20 meters. The triple 15, 20, 25 confirms it, since 225 plus 400 equals 625.
questions.hint: The radius to the touch point is perpendicular to the cable, so three lengths form a right triangle.

questions.topic: Two tangents from one external point
questions.learningObjective: state why two tangent segments from one external point are equal
questions.stem: Two straight ropes are tied from the same post standing outside a circular paddock, and each rope just touches the paddock fence at a different point. Which statement about the two rope lengths holds?

options.text: The ropes are the same length, because each is the hypotenuse of a matching right triangle
The ropes differ, since the two contact points sit in different places on the fence
options.misconception: believes where the rope touches changes its length for a fixed post

options.text: The ropes match only when the post lies level with the centre of the paddock
options.misconception: thinks the post must be on the line through the centre for the tangents to match

options.text: The ropes are the same length, and their contact points are opposite each other
options.misconception: believes equal tangents must touch diametrically opposite points of the circle

Both radii are perpendicular to the rope that touches there, so each rope with its radius makes a right triangle, and those two triangles share the same hypotenuse, the distance from the post to the centre, and the same other leg, the circle's radius. Two right triangles with an equal hypotenuse and an equal leg have equal third legs, so the ropes match. The contact points are symmetric about the line joining the post to the centre rather than opposite each other.
questions.hint: Each rope makes a right triangle with a radius, and both triangles share two side lengths.

questions.topic: Chord against secant segment
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a chord from a segment that passes through a circle
questions.stem: A straight stick is pushed partway into a round melon so that both of its ends finish outside the fruit, and a second stick is pushed all the way through so that both of its ends finish on the surface. How do the two sticks differ as segments of the circle?

options.text: The first is a secant segment, and the second is a chord with both ends on the circle
Both are chords, since any segment passing through the circle qualifies as one
options.misconception: treats every segment that meets a circle as a chord, endpoints ignored

options.text: The first is a chord, and the second is a diameter, because it crosses the centre
options.misconception: assumes a chord must be short and reserves the full width for diameters

options.text: The first is a chord, and the second is a secant, because it passes clean through
options.misconception: swaps the definitions of a chord and a secant segment

The first stick begins and ends outside, so it passes through the circle and is a secant instead, whose interior piece is the chord and whose two outer pieces belong to no chord at all. Whether a segment happens to cross the centre has no bearing on the naming, so a chord need not be a diameter and a diameter is simply the longest chord.
questions.hint: Check where each endpoint of the segment actually finishes.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Central against inscribed angle
questions.learningObjective: relate a central angle to an inscribed angle on the same arc
questions.stem: Two angles are drawn standing on one and the same arc of a circle. One of them has its vertex at the centre of the circle, and the other has its vertex out on the rim. How are the two measures related to each other?

options.text: The centre angle is twice the rim angle, because the centre spans the whole arc
The two angles are equal, because both of them stand on the same arc
options.misconception: believes a centre angle and a rim angle on one arc are equal, dropping the factor of two

options.text: The centre angle is half the rim angle, because the centre is nearer the arc
options.misconception: reverses the factor of two, shrinking the centre angle instead of doubling it

options.text: The two angles are supplementary, because together they close the circle
options.misconception: treats the pair as supplementary instead of as a doubling pair

questions.explanation: A rim angle standing on an arc measures half of that arc, while a centre angle standing on the same arc measures the arc in full. Since the arc is the shared quantity, the centre angle comes out exactly twice the rim angle. Moving the vertex to the centre is what creates the difference, because from the centre the arc subtends its whole measure whereas from the rim the same arc subtends half of it. Equality is the relation between two rim angles on one arc, never between a rim angle and a centre angle.
questions.hint: Compare what each vertex sees of the same arc.

questions.topic: Inscribed angle from a central angle
questions.learningObjective: halve a central angle to get the inscribed angle on the same arc
questions.stem: A circular plaza carries two marker posts on its rim, and the arc between them measured the shorter way round spans 140 degrees. A sighting line from the centre and a sighting line from a lamp post out on the rim both point at those two markers. How many degrees does the angle at the lamp post measure? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: The angle at the centre measures the full 140 degree arc, and an angle whose vertex sits on the rim measures half the arc it intercepts, so the lamp post angle is 140 divided by 2, which is 70 degrees. As a check, a rim angle standing on the other and larger arc would be half of 360 minus 140, that is half of 220, which is 110 degrees, and 70 plus 110 equals 180 as the two supplementary rim angles must.
questions.hint: The arc is the same in both cases, so one angle reads it whole and the other reads it in halves.

questions.topic: Angle where two chords meet inside
questions.learningObjective: add the two intercepted arcs and halve to find an interior chord angle
questions.stem: Two straight walkways cross at a point inside a circular park. The two arcs cut off on the far side of the crossing, one behind each walkway, measure 100 degrees and 40 degrees. How many degrees does the angle at the crossing between those two arcs measure? Report the number only.

Subtracting the arcs instead would give half of 60, which is 30 degrees, but the interior version of the rule adds them because both arcs lie on the far side of the crossing rather than one inside the other.

questions.topic: Cyclic quadrilateral
questions.learningObjective: state the opposite-angle relation in a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle
questions.stem: Four points lie on a single circle, and straight paths are built between them in order so that they enclose a four-sided field inside the park. What must be true of the interior angles of that field?

options.text: The two pairs of opposite interior angles each add up to 180 degrees
Opposite interior angles are equal to each other, as in a rectangle
options.misconception: believes a cyclic quadrilateral must have equal opposite angles

options.text: Every interior angle measures exactly 90 degrees in this configuration
options.misconception: assumes any quadrilateral on a circle has to be a rectangle

options.text: Each pair of adjacent interior angles adds up to 180 degrees
options.misconception: picks the wrong pair of corners, treating neighbours as supplementary

The individual angles need not be 90 degrees, so the field need not be a rectangle, and the supplementary pairing is between opposite corners rather than neighbours.

questions.topic: Tangent and chord angle
questions.learningObjective: state what a tangent-chord angle measures
questions.stem: A straight rope is pulled taut against a circular drum and touches it at one point, and a second straight line runs from that same point as a chord to another point on the drum. What does the angle between the rope and the chord measure?

options.text: Half the central angle standing on the same arc that the angle cuts off
The same as the central angle standing on that arc, with no halving
options.misconception: copies the centre angle instead of halving it for a vertex on the rim

options.text: The angle between the chord and the radius to the point of contact
options.misconception: measures from the radius rather than from the intercepted arc

options.text: Half the measure of the arc lying on the far side of the chord
options.misconception: intercepts the wrong arc, taking the complement rather than the arc named

questions.hint: The vertex is still on the rim, so the inscribed angle rule decides the measure.

questions.topic: Secant power relation
questions.learningObjective: use the shared product of two secants from one external point
questions.stem: A straight sightline from a hilltop tower meets a circular lake at the near shore 6 meters from the tower and leaves again at the far shore 14 meters from the tower, all along the one line. options.text: A circumcircle, whose radius runs from its centre to any one post
An incircle, whose radius is measured up to one of the field's sides
options.misconception: confuses the circle through the corners with the circle inside the sides

options.text: A semicircle, whose radius is one half of the longest side
options.misconception: assumes a circle through three points must be half a circle

An incircle is the other circle, lying inside the triangle and touching each side, so a fence that runs through the corners is the circumcircle and not that one.

questions.learningObjective: correct an inscribed angle copied from a central angle
questions.stem: A central angle of 128 degrees stands on an arc of a circle, and a student writes that the inscribed angle standing on that same arc also measures 128 degrees. What is the error in the student's answer?

options.text: A rim angle reads its arc in halves, so this one measures 64 degrees
A rim angle reads its arc doubled, so this one measures 256 degrees
options.misconception: doubles instead of halving, giving a value past a full turn

options.text: The two angles agree whenever they share one endpoint on the circle
options.misconception: believes a shared endpoint is what makes two different angles equal

options.text: The rim angle is the supplement of the centre angle, giving 52 degrees
options.misconception: borrows a supplementary rule that belongs to opposite arcs

questions.explanation: Both angles stand on one arc, but their vertices sit in different places, and that is the whole of the difference. A centre angle reads the arc in full, so it measures 128 degrees, while a vertex on the rim reads the same arc in halves, giving 64 degrees. As a check, the rim angle standing on the complementary arc is half of 360 minus 128, that is 116 degrees, and 64 plus 116 equals 180, which is what a supplementary pair of rim angles must give.
questions.hint: Track what each vertex sees of the same arc, and remember the halves.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Tangent length mistaken for radius
questions.learningObjective: correct a tangent length taken to be the radius
questions.stem: A post stands 20 meters from the centre of a circular pond of radius 16 meters, and a rope runs from the post and is just long enough to touch the shore. A student sets the rope length equal to the 16 meter radius. What is the error?

options.text: The radius and the rope are two legs of a right triangle, not one length
The radius and the rope are one and the same segment measured twice
options.misconception: assumes a tangent segment and the radius it touches are identical

options.text: The rope is really the 20 meter distance from the post to the centre
options.misconception: reads the external distance as though it were the tangent segment

options.text: The rope is the radius and the 20 meter distance added together
options.misconception: adds the two given lengths instead of building a right triangle

questions.explanation: The rope is a tangent, so the radius drawn to the contact point is perpendicular to it, and that right angle is what makes the three lengths a triangle. The 20 metre post-to-centre distance is the hypotenuse, the 16 metre radius is one leg, and the rope is the other leg, so the rope is the square root of 400 minus 256, which is 12 meters. Reporting 16 meters treats the two legs as if they were equal, which the right triangle has already ruled out.
questions.hint: Look for the right angle, then use the theorem rather than copying a side.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Closed cylinder surface, undercounted
questions.learningObjective: correct a cylinder surface total that omits the flat ends
questions.stem: Reporting the total surface area of a closed cylinder, a student works only from the wall expression, obtaining about 94.2 square inches from a radius of 3 inches and a height of 5 inches. What is missing from that answer?

options.text: The two flat circular ends, which together add 56.52 square inches
Nothing at all, since the wall expression already covers the whole drum
options.misconception: believes one formula already covers the wall and both ends together

options.text: The diameter, which was used in place of the radius in every term
options.misconception: swaps the radius for the diameter, doubling each part of the sum

options.text: A second copy of the curved wall, which the drum needs on its far side
options.misconception: assumes a cylinder has two separate curved walls to be counted

questions.explanation: A total surface area has to cover every face of the solid, and a closed cylinder has two flat circular ends as well as one curved wall. The wall expression gives 94.2 square inches, while the two ends together give 2 times 3.14 times 3 squared, that is 56.52 square inches, so the total is 150.72 square inches. A cylinder has a single wall, since the wall wraps all the way round, so there is no second wall to find and nothing in the wall expression stands in for the ends.
questions.hint: Count the faces, not the formulas: how many separate surfaces does the solid have?

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Why a perpendicular bisects a chord
questions.learningObjective: explain why a radius through a chord's midpoint is perpendicular to it
questions.stem: Explain why the segment joining the centre of a circle to the midpoint of a chord must be perpendicular to that chord, and say which known property of circles does the work.

answer.exemplar: Both ends of a chord lie on the circle, so both are the same distance from the centre, and that common distance is the radius. The segment from the centre to the chord's midpoint therefore has two pairs of points at equal distances from it: the centre and the midpoint each stand equally far from the two ends of the chord, and they are two distinct points. The set of all points equidistant from the two ends of a segment is exactly the perpendicular bisector of that segment, so the line through the centre and the midpoint is that perpendicular bisector, and it crosses the chord at a right angle. The property doing the work is the constancy of the radius, not anything about where the chord happens to sit.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Why a central angle is twice an inscribed one
questions.learningObjective: explain why a central angle measures double an inscribed angle on the same arc
questions.stem: Explain why a central angle standing on an arc measures exactly twice the inscribed angle standing on that same arc, and identify the step that forces the factor of two.

answer.exemplar: Draw the two radii from the centre to the two ends of the arc, together with the two chords from the rim vertex to those same ends. Four triangles now share the arc as a side, because the two triangles using the centre have all three sides equal to the radius, making each of them equilateral only when the arc is a sixth of the circle, while the two triangles using the rim vertex share the chord joining the two arc ends. In each of the four triangles the angle at the centre or at the rim vertex stands opposite the same side, and comparing the two isosceles triangles on the rim side shows the rim angle is half the centre angle by the isosceles base-angle relation. The cleanest statement is that the centre sits inside the wedge of the inscribed angle and splits it into two triangles, and the two rim angles produced by that split are each half the centre angle because the two radii are equal, so the whole inscribed angle is the sum of the two halves.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Why the unrolled diagonal is a true diagonal
questions.learningObjective: explain what a straight line across an unrolled cylinder wall measures
questions.stem: Explain why the diagonal of the rectangle obtained by unrolling a cylinder's curved wall is the length of a straight line wrapped around that wall, and say which two measurements set it.

answer.exemplar: Unrolling the wall is a rigid operation: every point of the curved surface keeps its true distance from every other point, so a straight line on the wall becomes a straight line on the flat sheet and keeps its length. The rectangle that results has one pair of sides equal to the cylinder's height, because the height never changes as one travels around the wall, and the other pair equal to the base's circumference, because travelling once around the wall covers exactly one full trip round the base. A corner-to-corner line on that sheet is therefore the diagonal of a rectangle with those two dimensions, found from the Pythagorean theorem as the square root of the circumference squared plus the height squared. Rolled back onto the cylinder, that same segment starts at a point on one rim, runs as a straight line across the wall, and finishes at a point on the other rim directly above where it started, having travelled once around the cylinder in the process.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Why two tangents from a point match
questions.learningObjective: explain why two tangent segments from one external point are equal
questions.stem: Explain, with reference to the right angles that appear, why the two tangent segments drawn from one external point to a circle are always the same length.

answer.exemplar: Let the external point be P, let the circle have centre O, and let the two points of contact be T1 and T2. Drawing the radii to those two points produces two right angles, at T1 and at T2, because a tangent is perpendicular to the radius drawn to its point of contact. Those two right angles together make the remaining two angles of the shape P, T1, O, T2 supplementary, so the angle at P and the angle at O add to 180 degrees, which places P and O on opposite sides of the chord T1 T2 and mirrors the two halves of the shape about the line OP. The two halves each have the same angle at P and the same angle at O, the same radius length down to T1 and T2, and the same shared hypotenuse OP, so they are congruent right triangles, and congruent triangles have equal corresponding sides, which gives PT1 equal to PT2. The equality therefore comes from the two right angles forcing a mirror image, and the shared hypotenuse is what lets the congruence criterion be invoked.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Finding an inradius
questions.learningObjective: order the steps for finding the radius of an inscribed circle
questions.stem: Four labelled statements describe how to find the radius of the circle inscribed in a triangle with sides of 13, 14, and 15 units. Put them in the order in which they must occur, earliest first.

options.text: Add the three sides together and halve the total to obtain the semiperimeter
Divide the area of the triangle by that semiperimeter to obtain the radius
Use the semiperimeter already found to work out the area of the triangle
Measure from a corner of the triangle straight down to the opposite side instead
options.misconception: believes a corner-to-side measurement belongs anywhere in this working

questions.explanation: The semiperimeter has to come first because the area formula in terms of three sides needs it as an input, so the semiperimeter of 21 units is established before the area can be computed. Once the area is known the radius is the quotient of area by semiperimeter, so the division comes last. Measuring from a corner to the opposite side never belongs in the working at all, since that is a different length from the perpendicular distance to a side, and doing it first would leave nothing for the later steps to use.
questions.hint: The area formula cannot be entered until the semiperimeter exists.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Finding a tangent length
questions.learningObjective: order the steps for finding a tangent segment from an external point
questions.stem: Four labelled statements describe how to find the length of a tangent drawn from a point 25 units from the centre of a circle of radius 15 units. Put them in the order in which they must occur, earliest first.

options.text: Recognise that the radius drawn to the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent
Take the 25 unit centre-to-point distance as hypotenuse and the 15 unit radius as a leg
Report the 15 unit radius as the tangent length, since both start at the centre
options.misconception: believes a leg of the right triangle equals the other leg

options.text: Apply the Pythagorean theorem to obtain the remaining leg, which is the tangent

questions.explanation: The perpendicularity has to be spotted first, because that right angle is the only reason the three lengths form a triangle and the only reason a theorem can be applied at all. Once the triangle is identified, the longest of the three lengths must be taken as the hypotenuse and the radius as one leg, which fixes the roles before any arithmetic. The theorem then produces the remaining leg, the tangent, and reporting the radius as the answer is a mistake the right triangle has already excluded, since a leg and the other leg need not match.
questions.hint: Nothing can be computed until the right angle that creates the triangle is found.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Finding a chord from a segment
questions.learningObjective: order the steps for finding the chord cut off by a given segment
questions.stem: Four labelled statements describe how to find the length of the chord cut off in a circle by a straight segment joining two points on the rim. Put them in the order in which they must occur, earliest first.

options.text: Measure the distance from the centre of the circle to that straight segment
Split the chord in half so the radius, the distance, and half the chord form a right triangle
Use the Pythagorean theorem on that right triangle to find the half-chord, then double it
Read the chord straight off as the diameter, since a chord spans the whole circle
options.misconception: believes every chord spans the whole circle and is therefore a diameter

questions.explanation: The distance from the centre to the segment is the input the whole method runs on, so it has to be found before anything else, and it is what tells you whether the segment sits at the centre or off to one side. Only then does splitting the chord at that foot point give a genuine right triangle, since the perpendicular from the centre to the chord is what lands on the midpoint. With the triangle in hand the theorem produces half the chord, and the last step doubles it back to the full chord, whereas reading the chord as the diameter is impossible for a segment that misses the centre.
questions.hint: The centre-to-segment distance is the input everything else depends on.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Finding a circumradius without a right angle
questions.learningObjective: order the steps for finding a triangle's circumradius from its sides and area
questions.stem: Four labelled statements describe how to find the circumradius of a triangle with sides of 13, 14, and 15 units and an area of 84 square units. Put them in the order in which they must occur, earliest first.

options.text: Multiply the three side lengths together to obtain the product of the sides
Divide that product by four times the area to obtain the circumradius
Take four times the area of the triangle as the second quantity in the quotient
Halve the longest side and report that as the radius, as one would for a right triangle
options.misconception: applies the right-triangle shortcut to a triangle with no right angle

questions.explanation: The quotient can only be assembled once both of its parts exist, so the product of the three sides is formed first and the four-times-area divisor is set up second. Dividing one by the other is then the only remaining step, and it yields 2730 over 336, which is 8.125 units. Halving the longest side belongs to the special case of a right triangle, where the circumcentre is the midpoint of the hypotenuse, and using it here would hide the dependence on the area that the general case requires.
questions.hint: Both terms of the quotient have to exist before the division can happen.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Angle standing on a diameter
questions.learningObjective: apply the corollary that a chord on a diameter subtends a right angle
questions.stem: A rope is stretched across a circular well so that its two ends sit at opposite ends of a diameter of the rim. A bird perches on the rim anywhere along the arc on the far side from the rope. What angle does the stretched rope make at the bird's feet?

options.text: 90 degrees, because the diameter makes the arc a semicircle of 180 degrees
45 degrees, because the bird sees half of the 90 degree right angle
options.misconception: halves an angle that the arc rule has already settled

options.text: 180 degrees, because the rope spans a full diameter of the well
options.misconception: reports the diameter's own length as an angle measure

options.text: 60 degrees, because a circle is usually divided into three equal parts
options.misconception: assumes the circle splits into thirds rather than following the arc

questions.explanation: The rope is a diameter, so it cuts the rim into two arcs of 180 degrees each, and the bird's angle stands on one of them with its vertex on the rim. An angle whose vertex is on the rim measures half the arc it intercepts, so the angle is half of 180, which is 90 degrees. The bird's position along the arc does not matter, since every inscribed angle standing on the same arc is equal, and the diameter is the special chord for which that half of 180 lands exactly on a right angle.
questions.hint: The arc the bird stands on is half the whole circle. Read it at the rim.

questions.subject: GEOMETRY
questions.topic: Radius as the fixed distance to the rim
questions.learningObjective: state what the radius measures for every point of a circle
questions.stem: A robot walks right around the rim of a circular track, and a post stands at the centre of the track. Which statement about the robot's distance from that post holds for its whole lap?

options.text: It stays the same at every point, and that fixed distance is the radius
It stays the same at every point, and that fixed distance is the diameter
options.misconception: calls the fixed centre-to-rim distance the diameter

options.text: It grows and shrinks, being least opposite the post and greatest beside it
options.misconception: believes the distance changes even though the track is a circle

options.text: It stays the same at every point, and that fixed distance is the circumference
options.misconception: names a length round the rim as a distance from the centre

questions.explanation: Every point of a circle is the same distance from the centre, and that constant distance is what the word radius names, so a robot on the rim never gets nearer to or further from the post. The diameter is twice this fixed distance, running from the centre out to the rim and on to the far side, and the circumference is the distance all the way around the rim rather than from the centre, so neither of those names the quantity in question. A distance that varied around a circle would mean the rim was not a circle at all.
questions.hint: Ask what single word names the fixed centre-to-rim distance.
